title: The soft X-ray dip of ASASSN-14ko stays 5.5 days before the UV peak from 2020 to 2024 and repeats at a constant 108.44-day period; the late flares are not a UV emission delay
abstract: Question: campaign studies found that the 2022-2026 flares of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko arrive up to 21 d later than the Payne et al. (2022) constant-Pdot ephemeris. Is this delay in the orbit or debris return, or in the UV/optical emission? Constant orbital decay is still allowed if the emission delay changes by at least 7 d. Approach: Payne et al. reported that the soft X-ray flux drops before each optical peak. We reduced all 398 public Swift XRT observations (2008-2026) and the daily XMM-Newton campaign of 2023 August-September without HEASoft or SAS. For each flare we fitted a box dip to the 0.3-2 keV counts (negative-binomial likelihood) and used the sharp drop (ingress) as a second clock, and we fitted the UVW2 peak on the same Swift visits. Results: five flares (2020-2024) have a clean ingress, measured to 0.4-0.8 d. XMM-Newton confirms the flare-30 ingress within 0.1 d. In the four flares with both markers, the ingress precedes the UV peak by 5.55 +/- 0.45 d. This lag changed by -0.04 +/- 1.20 d (95%: -2.4 to +2.3 d) from 2020 to 2023, while both markers moved about 6 d later relative to the published ephemeris. The X-ray ingress times alone fit a constant period of 108.44 +/- 0.06 d in 2020-2024 (residuals below 0.75 d; Pdot = +0.0003, 95%: -0.0008 to +0.0014). The published Pdot = -0.0026 is worse by delta chi2 = 28, 13 or 4.1 for a timing jitter of 0.5, 1 or 2 d. This test uses one marker type and has no inter-marker offset. Against the X-ray clock, earlier optical markers show the known fast period decrease before 2020, and the 2024-2025 ASAS-SN, SPHEREx and TESS markers arrive 3-8 d early, so the period became shorter again (about 106.8 d). Conclusion: the late flares are not a change of the UV/optical emission delay after the X-ray ingress. A 7-d delay change would have to act before the first debris arrival (a changing fallback time), or the period itself changed. The period changes in episodes, not as steady decay. Limitations: only five clean ingresses; quality cuts chosen after inspection of the light curves (sampling only); the curvature test depends on the jitter; post-2024 shifts use optical markers calibrated on two flares; no public data cover the 2026 flares.

display.caption: Top: O-C against the Payne et al. (2022) ephemeris for the Swift UVW2 peak (squares) and the soft X-ray ingress shifted by 5.5 d (circles; diamond: XMM-Newton). Both markers move about 6 d later from 2020 to 2023. Bottom: X-ray ingress minus UVW2 peak per flare; the mean is -5.5 d and it does not change.

Swift XRT 0.3-2 keV (top) and UVOT UVW2 (bottom) light curves of the five flares with a clean X-ray ingress, aligned on the ingress (solid line). Dashed line: UVW2 peak. Right: XMM-Newton EPIC-pn and OM data of flare 30.

O-C of all published ASASSN-14ko markers against the X-ray clock (constant P = 108.44 d, cycles 20-33, shaded). The period was longer before 2020, constant in 2020-2024, and shorter again after mid-2024. Dashed: Payne et al. (2022) ephemeris.

citations.reason: Its late ASAS-SN and TESS flares and constant period near 108 d in 2020-2026 agree with our independent X-ray clock (P = 108.44 d in 2020-2024).
We confirm the late flares with an X-ray marker. Our five ingress times do not constrain random period kicks of that size.
We use its Swift UVOT per-visit photometry and optical markers. Our X-ray clock supports its slower period decrease after 2021.
It allows constant decay if emission delays vary by at least 7 d. The fixed X-ray-to-UV lag shows that such a delay cannot be in the UV/optical stage after the X-ray ingress.
We compare its period-noise interpretation with the constant X-ray clock in 2020-2024 and the later decrease.
Its curvature evidence depends on a UV-to-optical offset. Our single-marker X-ray clock rejects the published curvature in 2020-2024 without such an offset, for jitter up to about 1 d.
We use its SPHEREx peak time of flare 37 in the O-C diagram against the X-ray clock.
Its finding of a changed flare rise width is compared with our unchanged X-ray-to-UV lag.
Energy-coupled clocks are discussed against a constant period for 13 cycles.
We adapt its Python Swift XRT and XMM-Newton PPS photometry code (MIT) and compare with the constant recurrence time of eRASSt J0456-20.
Origin of the Swift photometry code used through e2dd9320.
Related cross-source test of energy-coupled flare clocks.
Payne et al. 2021 (arXiv:2009.03321): published flare peak times of ASASSN-14ko.
Payne et al. 2022 (arXiv:2206.11278): ephemeris (P0 = 115.2 d, Pdot = -0.0026), published peak times, and the X-ray minimum about 5 d before the optical peak.
